stage.gloss: The idea of ‘mother’ in Proto-Indo-European — a language no one wrote, rebuilt by comparing its descendants.

steps.h: It begins in a voice we can’t hear
steps.p: Most of language history has no script at all. Proto-Indo-European — ancestor of Sanskrit and also of Latin, Greek and English — was never written. We know its words only because its children kept them.

stage.gloss: And in the south, an unrelated family — Dravidian — carries its OWN ancient word for mother. Tamil is not descended from Sanskrit.

steps.p: India spans genuinely unrelated language families. Indo-Aryan came in from the northwest; Dravidian was already here. They meet only far deeper, if at all. This split is the whole reason the story has two trees. See it in the DNA →

stage.gloss: Vedic Sanskrit says ‘mother’ — but for a thousand years it was chanted, not written. (Shown here in Devanagari, the script it would only later adopt.)

steps.h: Sanskrit — spoken long before it was written
steps.p: The Vedas were transmitted by memory for centuries. Sanskrit had no script of its own; it would later borrow whichever local one was at hand. Read the Hymn of Creation →

stage.gloss: The first script we can securely read: Brahmi, carved in Ashoka’s edicts. Here, the name ‘Bhārata’.

steps.h: One script appears — and everything descends from it
steps.p: Brahmi is attested in Ashoka’s edicts (~250 BCE) and deciphered only in 1837. Nearly every Indian script — and ~198 across Asia — grows from this single root.

stage.gloss: Brahmi forks: a Northern branch (→ Devanagari) and a Southern branch (→ Tamil, Telugu…). The letters look nothing alike — but share one logic.

steps.h: The one script forks north and south
steps.p: Palm-leaf writing rounded the southern scripts; the north kept angular forms and the headline bar. Different faces — same abugida skeleton underneath. Trace the script tree →

stage.gloss: ‘Mother’, today, across living languages and their own scripts. Indo-Aryan words trace to mātṛ; Dravidian ones to ammā — two roots, both alive, both written in Brahmi’s children.

steps.h: Six scripts, two roots, one screen
steps.p: The northern words still echo Sanskrit mātṛ; the southern ones still echo Dravidian ammā. Unrelated languages — written in scripts from one common ancestor. That is the journey in a single line.
